text.p: Australia's biggest insurer, the Australian Mutual Provident Society (AMP), posted a A$2.1 billion 1996 profit on Monday, boosted by a one-off payment from Britain's Pearl Group.

The profit outshone the A$1.9 billion in calendar 1995 as the insurance and funds management group sets itself up for a likely listing on the Australian, New Zealand and possibly British stock exchanges by late 1998.

AMP chief executive George Trumbull said 1996 overall was a "good year", as assets under management rose nine percent to A$94.5 billion, and premium income increased to A$7.4 billion from A$7.0 billion.
However, total income fell to A$16.0 billion from A$18.1 billion due to a decline in the return on the company's investments, reflecting less buoyant share markets.
The 1996 profit was lifted by a A$479 million one-off payment from its wholly-owned Pearl Group, following a settlement with British regulators of Pearl's "orphan estate".
This represents funds generated before 1965, in some cases as far back as the last century, which were never paid out by Pearl and have been earning interest ever since.
"It relates to a fairly small amount, but when you allow for compound interest over 30 years or so it can amount to quite a large figure," said deputy managing director Kerry Roberts.
A special bonus of A$630 million was also allocated from the settlement to more than two million Pearl with-profits life and pension policy holders.
Roberts said AMP would find it hard to match its 1996 profit figure in 1997 and pointed to the high return on capital, running at almost 24 percent in 1996.
"It's not likely to be sustained in the long term, although we would dearly like it to be so," he said.
Trumbull said AMP, which was recently beaten in bidding for Britain's Scottish Amicable , was interested in a number of other possible targets in Britain.
AMP also believed there were good opportunities to build businesses over the long term in the Asia/Pacific region, though not necessarily through acquisitions.
The insurer expected to be operating in four or five Asian countries within five years, and was considering a number of joint ventures.
Trumbull nominated India, Indonesia, the Philippines, Thailand and China as attractive countries.
He also said the group was expecting a vote by members on changing its structure from a mutual to a listed company in the final quarter of 1997.
AMP would rank among Australia's 10 largest listed companies, with more than two million likely shareholders and a market capitalisation of about A$10 billion, analysts say.
